issues.description: The manuscript explicitly states that the reported results were generated from randomized/dummy Qualtrics data, yet it proceeds to present inferential statistics and substantive conclusions as if they were empirical findings. Synthetic random data cannot provide evidence for or against the hypotheses; any p-values, effect sizes, or 'supported' hypotheses are artifacts of the simulation and sample size. This invalidates all substantive claims in the abstract and results.
issues.quote: [IMPORTANT: Results were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.] ... We generated a dummy set of samples in the Qualtrics survey (N = 1000) and found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect.

issues.description: The paper gives mutually incompatible statements about whether data collection was completed. It simultaneously says analyses are based on randomized placeholder data and that data collection was completed before analyses. This undermines transparency and makes it impossible to determine whether the preregistration and analyses were prospective, retrospective, or merely templated.
issues.quote: All measures and manipulations conducted for this investigation are reported, and data collection was completed before analyses.supplementary

issues.description: The procedure states that participants selected their preferred conditions. If taken literally, this means assignment to experimental conditions was not randomized. Self-selection destroys internal validity because participants choosing different conditions may differ systematically in attitudes, numeracy, prosociality, or prior beliefs, making causal interpretation impossible.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.description: The study is described as a within-subject design, but the reported analyses and cell counts are consistent with a between-subjects design. A true within-subject design would require repeated-measures modeling or mixed models accounting for subject-level dependence. If the design was actually between-subjects, the manuscript misreports the design; if it was within-subjects, the analysis is incorrect.
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables; donation and feeling variables as the dependent variables respectively. ... Residual ... Replication | 994

issues.description: The manuscript classifies the study as a 'close to very close replication' despite multiple major departures from the original: merging two separate experiments into one, changing the setting from lab to MTurk/online, updating victim stimuli, adding intervention to the joint condition, and changing the dependent variable from real donation behavior to hypothetical donation. These changes materially alter the operationalization and context, so the study cannot be straightforwardly interpreted as a direct close replication.
issues.quote: Replication classification | close to very close replication ... Updated victim information ... Intervention applied to the joint condition ... Imaginary donation ... Online survey

issues.subcategory: behavioral outcome replaced with hypothetical intention
issues.description: The original studies involved actual charitable giving with real money. This replication replaces that with a hypothetical self-report of how much participants would donate. Hypothetical donation intentions are not equivalent to costly donation behavior and are much more vulnerable to demand characteristics, social desirability, and reduced psychological realism. This substantially weakens construct validity and comparability with the target studies.
issues.quote: Imaginary donation Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.description: The operationalization of donation in the joint condition is unclear. Participants are exposed to both identifiable and statistical victim information, but the manuscript does not specify whether the donation is to the identifiable victim, to statistical victims, to both jointly, or how participants should allocate funds. Without a clearly defined target of donation, the dependent variable in the joint condition is ambiguous and not comparable to the original study.
issues.quote: The third group was considered as a joint condition provided with both statistical and identifiable victim information. ... Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s)

issues.description: Core experimental procedures and materials are not described in the manuscript itself. The paper largely redirects readers to external links and supplementary documents for the actual procedure and survey. The main text omits the exact manipulation wording, attention check, prior-knowledge screening, item wording, scale anchors, and randomization details. This prevents independent evaluation and replication.
issues.quote: The session of “Procedure” in the supplementary summarizes the procedure of the current replication study. For the full reported survey, please access the Qualtrics survey with the link below

issues.description: Basic sampling information is inconsistent or missing. Table 4 lists geographic origin and compensation as 'Not specified', yet elsewhere the manuscript says participants will be MTurk workers. Without clear recruitment source, inclusion criteria, compensation, and target population, the sample cannot be evaluated or reproduced.
issues.quote: Geographic origin | US American | Not specified | Not specified ... Compensation | US$5 | Not specified | Not specified ... Participants will conduct an online survey in Qualtrics on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform

issues.description: The manuscript states that participants were excluded for prior knowledge and failed attention checks, but it does not report how many participants were excluded, from what initial sample, or how these criteria were operationalized. Because the analyzed sample is simulated and the final cell counts sum neatly to 1000, it is also unclear whether exclusions were actually implemented in any meaningful way.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.description: The manuscript claims the sample size was determined by power analysis, but it does not provide the required elements of that analysis in the paper: target effect size, alpha, desired power, test family, or resulting required N. Instead, the analyzed sample appears to be an arbitrary set of 1000 generated responses. This prevents assessment of whether the study is appropriately powered for the stated hypotheses.
issues.quote: To obtain the minimal sample size required for this study, The sample size for this study was determined to ensure adequate statistical power for detecting the effects reported in the original study. The full report of power analysis can be found in the supplementary

issues.subcategory: wrong target effect for replication evaluation
issues.description: The manuscript says it will evaluate replication success using d = 0.48, which it previously identifies as the main effect of identifiability in the original Study 1. However, the central theoretical claim being replicated is the debiasing effect of deliberation, i.e., the interaction between identifiability and intervention. Using the wrong target effect mis-specifies the replication criterion and can lead to incorrect conclusions about success or failure.
issues.quote: We aim to study the effect of deliberative thinking on identifiable victim effect by comparing the replication effect with the original effect (d = 0.48, 95% CI [0.11, 0.84])

issues.description: The key interaction hypotheses require specific simple-effect tests: that explicit learning reduces donations for identifiable but not statistical victims, and that the implicit/joint presentation reduces donations to the identifiable victim. Instead, the manuscript reports an omnibus interaction and then a contrast between one cell (identifiable/no intervention) and the combination of all other cells. That contrast does not isolate the theorized simple effects and mixes theoretically distinct conditions.
issues.quote: 3 (Interaction effect) | Explicitly learning about the identifiable victim effect reduces donation to an identifiable victim but not to statistical victims ... 4 (Interaction effect) | Implicitly learning about the identifiable victim effect reduces donations to an identifiable victim ... we also conducted a t-test to study if the mean of identifiable/no intervention condition is different from the mean of combining other five conditions on donation.

issues.description: Donation is measured on a bounded 0-5 ordered scale. The original study included ordered probit regression, but the replication explicitly drops it. Reliance on ANOVA/t-tests alone for an ordered, bounded outcome reduces comparability with the original and may violate modeling assumptions depending on the observed distribution.
issues.quote: Ordered probit regression ... This test would not be conducted in the replication

issues.description: The manuscript conducts many inferential tests across multiple feeling variables, three effects per variable, post-hoc contrasts, and six correlations, but it only applies Bonferroni correction to some pairwise comparisons. There is no stated correction across the overall family of hypotheses. Given the large number of tests, isolated p-values near .05 (e.g., .045, .041) are especially vulnerable to false-positive error.
issues.quote: Note: Segregated feelings include being upsetting, being touched, being sympathetic, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and perceived impact of donation (extension)

issues.description: The paper analyzes an 'aggregated feelings' variable but does not explain how it was computed, whether items were standardized or averaged, whether they form a coherent scale, or whether internal consistency/reliability was acceptable. Aggregating heterogeneous items without psychometric justification can obscure effects or create uninterpretable composites.
issues.quote: Identifiability and intervention on aggregated feelings  Note: combine segregated feelings into one aggregated feeling

issues.description: The reported statistics are internally inconsistent. In multiple places, a comparison is labeled significant (p < .05) while the corresponding 95% confidence interval for Cohen's d includes zero. For a two-sided test, those should agree. This suggests miscalculated effect sizes, incorrect confidence intervals, or reporting errors, undermining confidence in the analyses.

The narrative interpretation of the donation means appears inconsistent with the descriptive statistics in Table 7. Table 7 shows higher donation means in the identifiable conditions than in the statistical conditions, but the text states the opposite and reports combined means that do not follow from the table. This raises concerns about coding mistakes, mislabeling of conditions, or incorrect interpretation of the analyses.
issues.quote: From Table 10, we noticed that there is a significant difference between identifiable and statistical victim condition, t(994)=-2.40, SE=0.13, p=.049, meaning that participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).

issues.description: The abstract claims support for the perceived-impact hypothesis in identifiable conditions, but the reported post-hoc results do not show a significant Identifiable vs Statistical difference. The only significant pairwise comparison is Statistical vs Joint. Therefore the abstract overstates and mischaracterizes the actual pattern of results.
issues.quote: Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.description: The manuscript is not review-ready: it contains placeholder notes, missing links, and sections explicitly marked as temporary simulations. This prevents full verification of materials and supplementary content and signals that the paper is incomplete.
issues.quote: Cloud folder for presentation (PPT and PDF) | <enter link here> ... Cloud folder for peer reviews | <enter link here>
